newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French family spending up, pessimism on jobs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French family spending up, pessimism on jobs.

text.p: Household spending on manufactured goods rose a healthy 1.9 percent in France in January, offering the government another opportunity to declare that the economy was starting to pick up after sluggish growth last year.
"This is another sign of the credibility of the rebound and of the good growth outlook for 1997," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis told Reuters on the sidelines of the annual farm show.
National statistics office INSEE said a 4.4 percent rise in retail spending -- in a month of post-Christmas discount sales -- more than compensated for a continued decline in car sales.
However, INSEE revised its initial December data to report a spending fall of 1.3 percent from a previous estimate of a more limited 0.8 percent decline.

The spending figures come after news on Tuesday of a record French trade surplus in 1996 and a survey conducted in January which showed a marked improvement industrialists' feelings about the outlook for increased production.
But it comes ahead of January unemployment data on Friday, which economists expect to show evidence of continuing deterioration. Unemployment is at a record 12.7 percent.

The rise in household spending prompted mixed reactions from economists, with some saying it heralded more robust demand in the first quarter of 1997, irrespective of the revision in the December data, but others remaining sceptical.

"This is a strong number. We're starting the first quarter with a very strong number on the demand side. A 0.2 percent INSEE (economic) growth forecast for the first quarter of 1997 looks too pessimistic, I think it could perhaps come in at 0.5 percent," said ABN Amro economist Philippe Brossard.

"We already knew car sales would continue to decline. The retail sector compensated. But seasonal sales started later than usual, on January 2. They sometimes start at the end of December, so this time this may explain the strong January number and the weak December one," he added.
David Naude, economist at JP Morgan in Paris, said: "First of all it's good news. It's clearly showing that the slide that took place in the fourth quarter has now come to an end."

"It doesn't tell us much about growth and genuine pickup, here we're seeing a recovery and we'll have to wait for the second quarter. But it's a sound reversal, coming quickly and robustly," he added.

Michala Marcussen at Societe Generale offered a more sober assessment. "This was very much in line with what we expected. A lot of it is because the (winter retail) sales period was pushed forward this year.

"Overall consumption remains fairly weak. The situation remains so very depressed on the labour market, consumer sentiment remains depressed. I do not see why the economy should pick up unless there is a positive impact from the tax reform."

The consumer spending figure followed the announcement on Tuesday that France set another trade surplus record of 122 billion francs ($21.7 billion) in 1996. A January survey showed a marked improvement among industrialists on the prospects of a pick-up in industrial production in the coming months.
A Reuter poll of 11 economists on Monday produced an average forecast of a 0.8 percent rise, with several saying the figure would be helped by retailers' winter discount sales.
Spending on cars, which has been suffering since the end of government car-buying incentives in September, fell 11.5 percent in January.
